title: Choosing a Pattern for Agentic AI

sections.heading: Everyday analogy
sections.body:
Think of a kitchen.

One cook doing everything is like a single-agent. It's fast, simple, and cheap.

A team of cooks is like multi-agent. One chops, one sauces, one plates. The team can handle a complex dinner better, but it is slower to coordinate and costs more to run.

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.body:
An AI agent is a helper that can make choices and do multi-step work on its own to reach a goal.

A design pattern is a layout for how agents work together and connect to the model and your data.

- Use single-agent when tasks are simple and you want low latency and low cost.
- Use multi-agent when tasks are open-ended, knowledge-intensive, and need higher accuracy.

Definitions: latency means wait time. Inference means one AI answer, and each one costs money. Human-in-the-loop means a person checks high-stakes work.

sections.heading: What can go wrong
sections.body:
Multi-agent can be more accurate, but it can also fail.

- More agents means more inference calls, so higher cost and longer wait.
- Teamwork is harder to manage and can get confused.

If usage grows 100x, cost and delay break first.

For high-stakes tasks, like money or safety decisions, you need human-in-the-loop or the system may make costly autonomous mistakes.

steps.narration: A goal-focused task arrives for the agent system.
Check task complexity and needs for latency, accuracy, and cost.
If simple, use single-agent for low wait and low cost.
If complex, use multi-agent team for better accuracy using external data.
If high-stakes, add a human to review before acting.

quiz.why: Single-agent is fast and cheap, good for simple tasks from the save.

quiz.q: What fails first if usage grows 100x for multi-agent?
options: Cost of inference calls and latency explode
quiz.why: More agents means many inference calls, so cost and wait time break first.
The save says high-stakes tasks need human oversight to avoid costly errors.
